title: Diwali Foods Move From Home Kitchens Onto Mainstream Canadian Store Shelves
excerpt: Ahead of Diwali's main day on Sunday, November 8, Canada's biggest grocers and food brands are merchandising mithai, pantry staples and Diwali campaigns in mainstream aisles, and their sales data show the festival window now outgrows the wider Indian food category.
body:
• Sales around Diwali in Canada have outgrown the wider Indian food category: Diwali timeframe volumes rose 20% since 2022, against 14% growth for the category over the same two years, according to AB World Foods, via Grocery Business.
  • Walmart Canada stocked its Diwali assortment in more than half of its stores, across 10% more stores than last year, including mithai for gifting and Sitara rice and lentils for festive cooking.
  • General Mills Canada ran a Diwali campaign for Cheerios and Nature Valley this year, with 'Light Up Your Cart' in-store displays across major Canadian retailers and public activations in Mississauga and Toronto.
  • For shoppers: Diwali staples and gifts are now in mainstream grocery aisles ahead of the festival's main day, Sunday, November 8, not only in South Asian specialty stores.

Diwali food in Canada is no longer confined to home kitchens and specialty shops. Ahead of the festival's main day on Sunday, November 8, the country's largest grocers and packaged-food brands are merchandising the festival in mainstream aisles, and the sales figures they cite explain why.

The sales case

Jeff David, vice president of sales for AB World Foods, told Grocery Business that Diwali timeframe volumes are outpacing the Indian food category, increasing 20% since 2022, against growth of 14% for the same category in the same two-year period. Retailers, he said, understand that festive holidays go beyond their historical cultural boundaries.

"When supported in flyer and in-store, it's an easy and food-focused way for all shoppers to feel inspired and want to participate."

— Jeff David, Vice President of Sales, AB World Foods

Conagra has adjusted its merchandising on the same logic. Lynne Strickler, the company's senior director of brand management and commerce marketing in Canada, told Grocery Business that because Diwali celebrations involve more visiting and snacking, Conagra now includes its everyday flavours in Diwali merchandising rather than focusing only on seasonal flavours. The company has also found that consumers who do not celebrate a given cultural event often join in by cooking its dishes at home.

AB World Foods is designing for that crossover shopper directly: clear packaging with easy-to-understand cooking instructions and shopping lists, and point-of-sale material and flyer executions with QR codes leading to recipes. The aim, David said, is an in-store display that can stop shoppers and inspire them to create an Indian meal at home.

What is on the shelves

Walmart Canada said its Diwali assortment was stocked in more than half of its stores, with even more products across 10% more stores than last year, alongside a larger Marketplace range online. Its gifting options include mithai and candy boxes. For home cooking and hosting, the retailer lists pantry staples including Sitara White Rice and Sitara Lentils, Great Value canola and vegetable oils and Great Value condensed milk, plus a newer savoury line, Great Value Masala Secret Recipe chips and popcorn.

"Diwali is such a meaningful time for many of our customers, and we're proud offer what they need to celebrate in one convenient place," said Sourabh Malik, vice president of food at Walmart Canada, in the retailer's announcement. The assortment extends beyond food to diyas and tealight candles, cookware, henna kits for a limited time, and, new in its announcement, kurta sets displayed at five stores in Ontario and sold through its Marketplace.

Brands join in

General Mills Canada built a full Diwali campaign this year around Cheerios and Nature Valley, LBB reported. The campaign, developed with Visionnaire, a Toronto-based agency specialising in multicultural advertising, is anchored by the tagline "Every firework needs a spark" and addresses the reality of celebrating Diwali away from extended family networks. Its retail program, Light Up Your Cart, placed customised in-store displays across major Canadian retailers, and its Diwali Spark Studio held public activations at Square One in Mississauga on October 23 and at Nathan Phillips Square in Toronto on October 24.

"For decades, General Mills has proudly championed the diverse communities that make up Canada," said Sonia Sharma, a senior manager at General Mills Canada, in the campaign report. "We know that balancing work, school and cultural traditions takes immense effort. This campaign reflects and celebrates a connection that is deeply rooted in South Asian Canadian households."

What has changed

The pattern across these moves is the same one CityNews Toronto described in its reporting on Diwali's wider audience in Canada: products once made at home or bought in community stores are now planned, promoted and displayed by national retailers and brands. Shoppers increasingly expect grocery retailers to reflect their cultural traditions in store offerings, Grocery Business reported, and the retailers' own numbers give them a commercial reason to keep expanding the assortment each year.

nri_angle: For South Asian Canadians, Diwali shopping no longer requires a special trip to a specialty store: mainstream grocers and national brands now stock and promote the festival's foods in the regular grocery run.
